articles.title: Strategy's bitcoin buying hinges on one number: STRC at $100
articles.description: What is happening Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, bought no bitcoin in the week of October 19 to 25. Instead it spent $204.9 million buying back its own STRC preferred shares, according to its October 26 filing with the SEC. Those buybacks have helped lift STRC to about $99.36, its highest level in roughly five months and just shy of its $100 par value. Social media accounts have run with the next step: Michael Saylor is "set to resume heavy Bitcoin buying" once STRC gets back to $100. That claim rests on a real, stated plan. Whether it plays out as "heavy" is a different question, and readers may get some answers soon. Strategy reports third-quarter results after the US close on Thursday, October 29, with a webinar at 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time. What STRC is and why $100 matters STRC, nicknamed Stretch, is a perpetual preferred share with a variable dividend that Strategy pays monthly. The dividend is adjusted to keep the price anchored near its $100 par value, and Strategy raised the rate to 12% during the summer slump. The $100 level matters because Strategy has said it will not sell new STRC below par. Above it, STRC becomes a fundraising tool again: Strategy can sell shares into the market and use the cash to buy bitcoin. It still has about $17.5 billion of STRC available to sell under its at-the-market (ATM) programme, and that figure has not moved in its weekly filings since at least June. Management has been explicit about the link. Chief executive Phong Le told Bloomberg TV on July 14 that once STRC gets back to par, Strategy will issue more and buy bitcoin. So the condition in the social media post is accurate. It is just not new. Bitcoin versus its own paper The recent filings show where Strategy's cash has been going. Newest first: Across those two weeks, Strategy spent about $18 on its own preferred shares for every $1 it spent on bitcoin. In the week in between, it bought 267 BTC for $22.1 million. It still holds 848,517 BTC at an average cost of about $75,446 per coin, so this is a change in the flow of new buying, not a retreat from the position. For bitcoin traders, that flow matters. Strategy has been the market's most reliable corporate buyer, and a week without it removes a familiar source of demand. Bitcoin slipped below $80,000 on October 27, with analysts at TradingKey pointing to both spot ETF outflows and the Strategy pause, though a single week does not prove cause and effect. Near par is not the same as par that holds Here is the catch in the "heavy buying" headline. Much of STRC's recovery has come from Strategy buying the shares itself. Its latest buyback works out to an average of about $99.06 a share, right where the five-month high sits. That support has a cost. After last week's buybacks, Strategy's USD Cash balance stood at $242.4 million, separate from a $4.83 billion USD Reserve set aside for preferred dividends and debt interest. The board lifted the preferred buyback authorisation from $2 billion to $3 billion on October 19, and about $957 million of it remains. The real test comes at $100. To fund bitcoin, Strategy has to sell new STRC to outside investors. If demand at the current dividend is thinner than hoped, fresh issuance could push the price back below par and send Strategy back to buying its own paper. Saylor's informal goal of regaining par by September 8 has already come and gone, which suggests the last few dollars are the hardest. What to watch next Tonight's earnings call. Listen for any update on the STRC dividend rate, the buyback budget and the conditions for restarting STRC sales. A clear timetable would matter more than another round of "once we get to par". STRC at $100 without help. The stronger signal is STRC holding at or above par in weeks when Strategy is not buying it back. Price support from the issuer itself proves little about outside demand. Monday's filings. Strategy reports weekly. The line to check is STRC shares sold under the ATM. While that reads zero, the big funding channel is still shut, whatever the headlines say. Bitcoin purchase size. Buying funded only by common stock sales has recently run at tens of millions of dollars a week. Heavy buying, by Strategy's own past standards, would be a much bigger number. What would change the view: confirmed STRC issuance at par followed by sizeable bitcoin purchases in the same filing. Until then, treat the $100 level as a door that is nearly open, not one Strategy has walked through. The practical takeaway for bitcoin traders: Strategy's weekly filing is one of the clearest demand signals in the market. It is worth reading alongside ETF flows, rather than relying on what social media says the filing will show. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: HSBC shares slide almost 7% as revenue misses and wealth stalls despite 32% profit jump
articles.description: The sell-off shows how much was already priced into HSBC after a strong run. Without a guidance upgrade, a revenue miss and stalled wealth growth were enough to trigger profit-taking. The read-across for Hong Kong and Asian banks is margin pressure: costlier time deposits threaten interest income just as the Fed’s hiking path keeps funding costs high. Oil matters indirectly, since inflation and rate uncertainty linked to the Iran war is weighing on bank valuations broadly, and HSBC is already setting aside provisions for the Middle East conflict. The Basel 3.1 capital boost from January 2027 gives HSBC room to expand buybacks, which could limit further downside once the disappointment fades. --- Earlier: Goldman: Markets selling US banks on higher rates, but income guidance rises into 2027 HSBC delivered a big profit jump and another $1 billion buyback, but a revenue miss, flat wealth income and no upgrade to its targets were enough to send the shares sharply lower. Summary: HSBC shares fell almost 7% on Tuesday after third-quarter revenue of around $18.6 billion missed forecasts of roughly $19.1 billion, and adjusted EPS of $2.10 missed $2.22. Pre-tax profit rose 32% to around $9.6 billion, helped by the absence of last year’s legal provisions. Excluding notable items, it rose about 10% to around $10 billion. Wealth revenue was flat at around $2.7 billion after strong growth in the first half. Net interest income rose 6% but was slightly below expectations. Deposit competition in Hong Kong and the UK is rising, with time deposits at 38% of the Hong Kong mix. Guidance was reaffirmed, not raised: banking NII of at least $46 billion in 2026 and a RoTE of at least 17% for 2026 to 2028. HSBC announced a new buyback of up to $1 billion. CET1 eased to 13.9%, with Basel 3.1 expected to add 40 to 50bp from January 2027. HSBC shares fell almost 7% on Tuesday after third-quarter revenue missed forecasts and its wealth business stalled, overshadowing a 32% jump in pre-tax profit to around $9.6 billion and a fresh buyback of up to $1 billion. Revenue came in at around $18.6 billion for the July to September quarter, short of the roughly $19.1 billion analysts had expected, while adjusted earnings per share of $2.10 missed the $2.22 consensus. Pre-tax profit was broadly in line with estimates, but the headline gain was flattered by the absence of legal provisions booked a year earlier. Excluding notable items, profit rose about 10% to around $10 billion. The weakest spot was wealth, one of the bank’s main growth engines. Wealth revenue was flat at around $2.7 billion, after year-on-year growth of 15% and 23% in the first two quarters, although net new money in Asia remained strong at around $38 billion for the quarter. Net interest income rose 6% to around $9.3 billion, slightly below expectations, with the net interest margin, the gap between what the bank earns on loans and pays on deposits, steady at 1.57%. Analysts flagged rising competition for deposits in Hong Kong and the UK as a pressure point. Time deposits, which pay savers higher rates, rose to 38% of HSBC’s Hong Kong deposit mix, a shift that tends to erode margins. Management said deposit competition in Hong Kong was the bigger factor for interest income. Investors had also hoped for upgrades. HSBC reaffirmed, rather than raised, its guidance for banking net interest income of at least $46 billion this year and a return on tangible equity of at least 17% from 2026 to 2028, with revenue growth reaching 5% by 2028. Chief financial officer Pam Kaur acknowledged that the market sometimes expects guidance or targets to be lifted. Credit quality held up. Expected credit losses fell 17% to around $800 million, helped by lower charges on Hong Kong commercial real estate, while the bank’s nine-month provisions include allowances for uncertainty linked to the Middle East conflict. The CET1 capital ratio slipped to 13.9%. HSBC expects incoming Basel 3.1 rules to add 40 to 50 basis points to that ratio from January 2027, against a 14% to 14.5% target range, and said buybacks remain its preferred way to return surplus capital. The reaction leaves HSBC needing to show that wealth momentum can recover and that deposit costs will not eat further into margins when it reports full-year results. This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

articles.title: Growing List of Firms Object to OKX-ICE Tokenized Stock Plans
articles.description: Intel, Oracle, IBM and IonQ have joined a growing list of companies objecting to having tokenized versions of their shares traded through OKX and Intercontinental Exchange's blockchain venture, bringing the total number of objections to 26. About 37% of the companies on OKXICE's original list have now opted out, according to CoinDesk. From the report: The four companies were named in an updated public notice (PDF) dated Monday, Oct. 26, from OKXICE, the two firms' joint venture. They join earlier objectors including Microsoft, Alphabet, Goldman Sachs, Cisco and Wells Fargo. The growing list underscores a hurdle for OKXICE and the SEC's new framework for tokenized stock trading: building a market that issuers are willing to join. The agency's five-year "Innovation Exemption" gives qualifying venues room to test round-the-clock blockchain-based trading of stocks, and it also gives public companies an option to block their shares from being offered. OKXICE issued its initial public notice on Oct. 4, outlining plans to use Uniswap v4 liquidity pools on OKX's XLayer blockchain, with transactions settled in stablecoins. The venue would use automated market makers -- software that executes trades through pools of assets rather than matching buyers and sellers through a conventional order book. Under the framework, venues must notify issuers and give them 30 days to object before offering tokenized versions of their shares. Read more of this story at Slashdot.
